title: Using Political Power to Protect Students from Using AI in Education
author: Scott Cunningham
summary: High school English teacher Scott Cunningham criticizes ISTE+ASCD's "Profile of an AI-Ready Graduate" and welcomes Florida's new State Board of Education rule on AI in K-12 schools. He argues that the six proposed standards, which have students use AI as learner, problem-solver, researcher, connector, synthesizer and storyteller, hand over the very uniquely human capacities that school exists to develop. Beyond learning, he contends that habituating students to reach for AI whenever work feels hard damages character formation, likening AI's illusion of omnipotence to the serpent's promise to be like God. Florida's rule, with its opt-in default, protection of teacher judgment, verification of student-authored work and effectiveness review, supplies healthy friction, though he finds it too bureaucratic and focused on assessment. He concludes that AI can aid learning only after students have the knowledge to question and evaluate it, which is what schools should be supplying.
points: Cunningham notes the irony that the skills ISTE+ASCD would assign to AI are precisely the uniquely human skills the framework claims to value.
He describes the standards as bolting training wheels onto every hard task, removing the struggle where learning happens.
The formation argument is theological: wrestling with difficulty teaches limits and discipline, while AI offers an illusion of omnipotence.
Florida's rule makes non-use the default, requires comparable non-AI alternatives and bars AI from simulating friendship with students.
He would strengthen the rule by forbidding districts from requiring teachers to assign AI-dependent work.
quotes: However, I would have no idea if it were being used to positive effect or not if I did not already have a substantial knowledge or experience of the thing that I was using it for.

There’s a terrific irony in the fact that these areas where ISTE is proposing AI be used are, in fact, “uniquely human skills.” Gaining and developing these capacities is part of how we realize the unique nobility of humanity.

Because it essentially is dictating that students would learn to use AI to support most of their learning functions, completely disregarding the reality that the whole reason students are in school is for them to be taught
This set of standards essentially proposes AI as a safety net beneath the students, training wheels to bolt on whenever a certain task feels hard.

It’s in the difficult wrestling with hard tasks, especially in formative school years, that we learn that we have limits. We build character and discipline by exerting ten more minutes of concentration on a difficult problem when it would be easy to just turn in the work as is and call it “good enough.
It reflects a tendency to think of the significance of the integrity of student work primarily in terms of assessment, when it’s the integrity of the day to day classwork that learning depends on.

And AI certainly can be an excellent tool to improve one’s learning, but only after one has gained sufficient knowledge and thinking skill to know what questions to ask and how to evaluate the responses.
